question: What intrapartum precaution is typically practiced to manage risks associated with vulval varicosities during delivery?

options.A: Administering intravenous anticoagulants throughout the first stage of labor
options.B: Performing a routine scheduled cesarean section for all diagnosed cases
options.C: Placing a continuous pressure pack over the perineum during contractions
options.D: Avoiding incisions directly through enlarged veins if an episiotomy is performed

explanation: Cutting into a dilated varicosity risks severe bleeding, so providers carefully angle or avoid episiotomy incisions when large vessels are present. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h7)

question: What is the primary maternal risk associated with vulval varicose veins during the intrapartum period?

options.A: Complete uterine rupture during the second stage of labor
options.B: Immediate development of systemic septic shock
options.C: Permanent paralysis of the lower extremities
options.D: Increased bleeding if vessels rupture or are lacerated

explanation: The high volume of blood within these fragile superficial vessels can lead to significant localized hemorrhage if trauma or tearing occurs during birth. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h7)

question: What is the appropriate initial nursing action if a vulvar varix ruptures during the immediate postpartum period?

options.A: Prepare the patient for immediate surgical ligation in the operating room
options.B: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter to relieve bladder pressure
options.C: Administer oral analgesics and apply a warm water soak
options.D: Apply direct firm pressure to the bleeding site and notify the clinician

explanation: Direct pressure is the most effective first-line emergency measure to control surface bleeding from superficial venous ruptures while awaiting medical assistance. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h8)

question: Which complication is characterized by a firm, painful, cord-like swelling in a previously soft vulvar vein?

options.A: Superficial thrombophlebitis
options.B: Necrotizing fasciitis
options.C: Pelvic inflammatory disease
options.D: Bartholin gland abscess

explanation: Inflammation combined with localized clot formation inside a superficial vein creates a firm, tender cord palpable in the tissue. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h8)

question: Which embryonic structures are responsible for the development of the female internal reproductive organs?

options.A: Gonadal ridges
options.B: Urogenital sinus
options.C: Müllerian ducts
options.D: Wolffian ducts

explanation: The female internal genitalia, including the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina, originate from the paramesonephric or müllerian ducts during fetal development. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h1)

question: What is the primary structural difference between a bicornuate uterus and a septate uterus?

options.A: A septate uterus possesses two distinct cervices whereas a bicornuate uterus shares a single unified cervix.
options.B: A bicornuate uterus features a normal external fundal contour whereas a septate uterus has a divided outer surface.
options.C: A septate uterus has a normal external fundal contour whereas a bicornuate uterus displays an external fundal cleft.
options.D: A bicornuate uterus involves complete absence of one müllerian duct while a septate uterus has both ducts fused.

explanation: The external surface of a septate uterus appears smooth and normal because the ducts fused properly, whereas a bicornuate uterus shows a distinct dip or indentation at the fundus due to incomplete fusion. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h1)

question: What are benign smooth muscle tumors of the uterus commonly known as?

options.A: Adenomyomas
options.B: Leiomyomas
options.C: Lipoleiomyomas
options.D: Endometriomas

explanation: Uterine fibroids are scientifically termed leiomyomas, representing benign monoclonal neoplasms originating from the smooth muscle cells of the myometrium. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h2)

question: Which acquired uterine condition is most directly associated with a history of aggressive dilation and curettage following childbirth?

options.A: Diffuse adenomyosis
options.B: Uterine leiomyomatosis
options.C: Endometrial hyperplasia
options.D: Asherman syndrome

explanation: Aggressive or deep curettage damages the basal layer of the endometrium, leading to the formation of intrauterine adhesions and scar tissue characteristic of Asherman syndrome. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h2)

question: Why do submucosal fibroids typically cause heavy menstrual bleeding whereas subserosal fibroids usually do not?

options.A: Submucosal fibroids secrete excessive amounts of human chorionic gonadotropin into the bloodstream.
options.B: Submucosal fibroids directly distort and increase the surface area of the bleeding endometrial cavity.
options.C: Subserosal fibroids prevent the ovaries from producing adequate progesterone to stabilize the lining.
options.D: Subserosal fibroids physically block the internal cervical os and trap the menstrual blood.

explanation: Because submucosal fibroids sit directly beneath the endometrium, they expand the mucosal surface and interfere with local vascular compression, directly leading to heavy menstrual bleeding. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h3)

question: What term describes the condition where menstrual blood is trapped behind an anatomical obstruction without escaping externally?

options.A: Menometrorrhagia
options.B: Hypomenorrhea
options.C: Polymenorrhea
options.D: Cryptomenorrhea

explanation: Cryptomenorrhea occurs when menstruation happens normally inside the reproductive tract, but an outflow obstruction prevents the blood from exiting the body. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h3)

question: What imaging technique is considered the gold standard for accurately mapping complex congenital müllerian anomalies?

options.A: Computed tomography scan
options.B: Plain pelvic radiography
options.C: Magnetic resonance imaging
options.D: Abdominal ultrasonography

explanation: MRI provides superior soft-tissue contrast and multiplanar imaging, making it the most accurate modality for delineating complex uterine malformations and pelvic anatomy. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h4)

question: A clinician wants to evaluate both the patency of the fallopian tubes and the interior contours of the uterine cavity during an infertility workup. Which test is most appropriate?

options.A: Endometrial biopsy
options.B: Transabdominal ultrasound
options.C: Hysterosalpingography
options.D: Diagnostic laparoscopy

explanation: An HSG utilizes radiopaque contrast injected through the cervix to outline the uterine cavity and demonstrate spill through the fallopian tubes, assessing both structures simultaneously. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h4)

question: Which surgical procedure removes uterine fibroids while leaving the uterus intact for future childbearing?

options.A: Hysterectomy
options.B: Trachelectomy
options.C: Cervicectomy
options.D: Myomectomy

explanation: Myomectomy is the surgical removal of leiomyomas specifically designed to preserve the structural integrity of the uterus and maintain the patient's reproductive potential. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h5)

question: What is the primary objective of prescribing GnRH agonists prior to surgical removal of large uterine fibroids?

options.A: To induce immediate and permanent menopause in the patient
options.B: To reduce the size and vascularity of the fibroids
options.C: To permanently eliminate the growth of smooth muscle cells
options.D: To prevent the development of postoperative pelvic infections

explanation: GnRH agonists create a hypoestrogenic state that shrinks fibroid volume and decreases intraoperative blood loss, making surgical excision safer and easier. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h5)

question: How do submucosal fibroids most commonly interfere with the establishment of a successful pregnancy?

options.A: By disrupting the endometrial lining and preventing proper embryo implantation
options.B: By destroying circulating progesterone required to maintain corpus luteum function
options.C: By inducing premature closure of the fallopian tubes bilaterally
options.D: By blocking the ovaries from releasing mature oocytes during ovulation

explanation: Submucosal fibroids distort the cavity and alter the local endometrial environment, making it hostile for a blastocyst to implant successfully. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h6)

question: Which complication is a pregnant patient with a bicornuate uterus most statistically at risk for developing?

options.A: Ectopic tubal pregnancy
options.B: Gestational diabetes
options.C: Placenta accreta spectrum
options.D: Preterm delivery

explanation: Congenital uterine malformations like the bicornuate uterus limit the space available for the growing fetus, significantly increasing the incidence of preterm labor and delivery. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h6)

question: What is a primary nursing priority when caring for a patient experiencing heavy menstrual bleeding secondary to uterine fibroids?

options.A: Inserting an indwelling urinary catheter to monitor output
options.B: Assessing for signs and symptoms of iron-deficiency anemia
options.C: Administering intravenous broad-spectrum prophylactic antibiotics
options.D: Encouraging complete bed rest throughout the menstrual cycle

explanation: Chronic heavy menstrual bleeding depletes iron stores, making fatigue, pallor, and low hemoglobin levels critical assessment parameters for nurses managing these patients. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h7)

question: A patient scheduled for a hysteroscopic resection of a submucosal fibroid expresses deep anxiety, fearing the procedure will cause instant menopause. How should the nurse respond?

options.A: Reassure her by stating that most women do not experience any physical changes whatsoever after pelvic surgery.
options.B: Tell her that only a total abdominal hysterectomy will cause immediate menopause symptoms.
options.C: Explain that hysteroscopic resection preserves the ovaries and uterus, so natural hormone production and menstruation will continue.
options.D: Confirm her fears and advise her to discuss hormone replacement therapy options immediately with the attending surgeon.

explanation: Correcting misconceptions is a key nursing duty; hysteroscopic procedures target the uterine cavity and do not remove or damage the ovaries, which control menopausal status. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h7)

question: What is the primary anatomical structure involved in endometritis?

options.A: The distal portion of the fallopian tubes
options.B: The inner mucosal lining of the uterus
options.C: The muscular middle layer of the uterine wall
options.D: The fibromuscular canal of the lower reproductive tract

explanation: Endometritis specifically refers to inflammation of the endometrium, which forms the inner mucosal layer of the uterine cavity. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h1)

question: When does endometritis most frequently develop in clinical practice?

options.A: During the mid-follicular phase
options.B: Immediately following childbirth
options.C: At the onset of menopause
options.D: Right before menses begins

explanation: The postpartum period presents the highest risk for bacterial invasion due to the open wound left at the placental implantation site. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h1)

question: Which surgical procedure carries the highest risk for developing postpartum endometritis?

options.A: Vacuum extraction
options.B: Manual removal of placenta
options.C: Episiotomy repair
options.D: Cesarean section delivery

explanation: Surgical opening of the uterus introduces a direct pathway for operating room and skin contaminants into the uterine cavity. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h2)

question: Why does prolonged rupture of membranes predispose a patient to uterine infection?

options.A: It causes immediate necrosis of the myometrium
options.B: It increases the systemic pH of maternal blood
options.C: It removes the protective barrier preventing ascending vaginal bacteria
options.D: It halts the production of normal maternal hormones

explanation: The amniotic membranes normally seal the intrauterine environment; once ruptured, microorganisms have direct access to the uterine cavity. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h2)

question: What type of cellular infiltrate is the hallmark diagnostic feature of chronic endometritis?

options.A: Basophils
options.B: Plasma cells
options.C: Eosinophils
options.D: Neutrophils

explanation: The presence of plasma cells in the endometrial stroma is the definitive histological marker distinguishing chronic endometritis from the acute neutrophilic form. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h3)

question: How does acute postpartum endometritis typically initiate its pathological process?

options.A: Bacteria ascend from the lower genital tract to colonize placental sites
options.B: Viral replication destroys the basal layer of the endometrium
options.C: A systemic autoimmune reaction targets uterine smooth muscle
options.D: Hormonal withdrawal triggers localized sterile tissue necrosis

explanation: Microorganisms travel upward from the vagina and multiply rapidly on the exposed, nutrient-rich placental bed after delivery. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h3)

question: Which symptom is most characteristic of postpartum acute endometritis?

options.A: Foul-smelling or purulent lochia
options.B: Severe hypertension and visual disturbances
options.C: Complete cessation of vaginal bleeding
options.D: Painless enlargement of the lower extremities

explanation: Bacterial proliferation within the necrotic decidua produces infected, foul-smelling, and discolored lochia. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h4)

question: A postpartum patient on day three exhibits a temperature of 38.8°C, lower abdominal pain, and a boggy, tender uterus upon palpation. What condition do these findings point toward?

options.A: Normal lochia rubra
options.B: Endometritis
options.C: Postpartum depression
options.D: Cystitis

explanation: Fever, uterine tenderness, and a boggy fundus in the early postpartum period are the classic triad pointing directly toward acute endometritis. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of ordering a pelvic ultrasound for a suspected case of postpartum endometritis?

options.A: To detect retained products of conception
options.B: To visualize ovarian hormone production
options.C: To assess kidney perfusion and urine output
options.D: To measure exact blood pressure fluctuations

explanation: Ultrasound imaging helps identify any remaining placental tissue in the uterine cavity that might be fueling the infection. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h5)

question: Why are routine transcervical endometrial cultures generally avoided in acute postpartum endometritis?

options.A: They easily become contaminated by normal vaginal flora during insertion
options.B: Laboratory equipment cannot process bacterial growth from uterine tissue
options.C: They cause immediate rupture of the myometrium
options.D: The procedure requires general anesthesia in an operating room

explanation: Passing a swab through the vagina and cervix picks up commensal organisms, making it difficult to isolate the true causative pathogen of the infection. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h5)

question: What is the typical pharmacological approach for treating acute postpartum endometritis?

options.A: Single-dose oral antifungal medications
options.B: Topical antiseptic creams applied to the cervix
options.C: Intramuscular long-acting synthetic progestins
options.D: Broad-spectrum combination intravenous antibiotics

explanation: Because the infection is polymicrobial, potent intravenous combination antibiotics targeting aerobes and anaerobes are required immediately. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h6)

question: When can intravenous antibiotic therapy for uncomplicated endometritis typically be discontinued?

options.A: Immediately upon the first normal temperature reading
options.B: Only after completing a mandatory 14-day hospital stay
options.C: Once lochia color completely transitions to alba
options.D: After the patient remains afebrile for 24 to 48 hours

explanation: Clinical guidelines recommend continuing IV antibiotics until the patient shows sustained clinical improvement and remains fever-free for a specified window. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h6)

question: A postpartum client diagnosed with endometritis is receiving IV antibiotics and analgesics. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate to include in her immediate care plan?

options.A: Limiting infant visitation to prevent transmission of maternal bacteria
options.B: Strict bed rest in a Trendelenburg position for the duration of the hospital stay
options.C: Encouraging early ambulation as tolerated to promote lochia drainage and circulation
options.D: Withholding all oral fluids until antibiotic therapy is fully completed

explanation: Early ambulation helps uterine drainage and decreases the risk of deep vein thrombosis, which is elevated during postpartum infections. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h7)

question: What is a key instructional point when educating a recovering endometritis patient about perineal care?

options.A: Use harsh antiseptic soaps for internal vaginal irrigation daily
options.B: Wipe from front to back and change sanitary pads frequently
options.C: Avoid changing sanitary pads more than twice a day
options.D: Apply dry heat packs directly to the internal mucosal walls

explanation: Proper hygiene prevents the introduction of additional fecal bacteria into the healing reproductive tract. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h7)

question: Which complication is associated with chronic or severe intrauterine infection leading to scarring and potential infertility?

options.A: Cervical ectropion
options.B: Asherman syndrome
options.C: Vaginal vault prolapse
options.D: Gestational trophoblastic disease

explanation: Intrauterine adhesions or scarring resulting from severe or chronic endometrial damage form Asherman syndrome, which impairs future fertility. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h8)

question: What pathological process characterizes septic pelvic thrombophlebitis, a serious complication of uterine infections?

options.A: Rapid rupture of the ovarian follicles during menses
options.B: Blood clot formation in pelvic veins accompanied by bacterial infection
options.C: Complete obstruction of the ureters by external scarring
options.D: Widespread necrosis of the abdominal wall musculature

explanation: Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis involves thrombosis of the pelvic venous system combined with proliferating infection, posing a high risk for septic emboli. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h8)

question: What is the primary defining characteristic of endometriosis?

options.A: Complete absence of cyclical ovarian hormone production
options.B: Presence of endometrial-like tissue outside the uterine cavity
options.C: Bacterial infection of the inner lining of the uterus
options.D: Hypertrophy of the myometrial smooth muscle layer

explanation: Endometriosis is characterized strictly by the abnormal growth of tissue resembling the endometrium in locations outside the uterus. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h1)

question: Why do ectopic endometrial implants cause chronic pain and inflammation?

options.A: Trapped menstrual-like bleeding causes localized irritation and scarring
options.B: Ovarian cysts rupture continuously throughout the luteal phase
options.C: Direct invasion of the spinal nerves by endometrial glands
options.D: The lesions release high levels of bacterial toxins into the pelvic cavity

explanation: Because ectopic tissue bleeds during menstruation without an exit route, the trapped blood incites an inflammatory reaction leading to fibrosis and adhesions. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h1)

question: What is the name of the theory suggesting endometrial tissue travels backward through the fallopian tubes during menstruation?

options.A: Sampson's theory of retrograde menstruation
options.B: Coelomic metaplasia developmental model
options.C: Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser hypothesis
options.D: Vascular dissemination and embolization theory

explanation: Sampson's theory proposes that menstrual debris flows backward through the fallopian tubes and implants in the pelvic cavity. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h2)

question: What factor best explains why most women with retrograde menstruation do not develop clinical endometriosis?

options.A: Peritoneal fluid in healthy women contains high levels of pure progesterone
options.B: An effective immune response clears the ectopic cells from the peritoneal cavity
options.C: The endometrium in these women completely lacks glandular epithelium
options.D: Retrograde flow only occurs after complete surgical menopause

explanation: Immune surveillance and peritoneal macrophage activity typically clear shed endometrial cells in healthy individuals, preventing implantation. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h2)

question: What term is commonly used to describe ovarian endometriomas filled with old, dark blood?

options.A: Serous cystadenomas
options.B: Chocolate cysts
options.C: Dermoid cysts
options.D: Theca lutein cysts

explanation: Ovarian endometriomas accumulate chronic menstrual-like blood that turns dark brown over time, earning them the descriptive name chocolate cysts. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h3)

question: A patient asks why her surgeon reported severe Stage IV endometriosis despite her main complaint being mild discomfort. What is the most accurate nursing explanation?

options.A: Endometriosis pain disappears completely once the disease reaches advanced stages
options.B: Staging measures the amount of scar tissue and implant spread, not the exact level of pain
options.C: Stage IV disease always produces less severe nerve irritation than early stages
options.D: The staging system only evaluates hormone levels rather than actual physical implants

explanation: The rASRM classification scores anatomical extent and adhesions rather than symptom severity, meaning low stages can be very painful and high stages silent. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h3)

question: Which clinical symptom is most characteristic of deep infiltrating endometriosis involving the uterosacral ligaments?

options.A: Painless post-menopausal vaginal bleeding
options.B: Bilateral lower extremity edema
options.C: Deep dyspareunia during sexual intercourse
options.D: Upper right quadrant abdominal tenderness

explanation: Implants in the posterior cul-de-sac or uterosacral ligaments are repeatedly compressed during coitus, resulting in deep dyspareunia. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h4)

question: A young adult client presents with progressive, severe menstrual cramps that no longer respond to ibuprofen. What is the most appropriate initial nursing interpretation?

options.A: The client is likely experiencing primary dysmenorrhea requiring psychological referral
options.B: This pattern indicates normal physiological maturation of the menstrual cycle
options.C: Analgesic tolerance has developed, requiring immediate opioid initiation
options.D: These symptoms strongly suggest secondary dysmenorrhea such as endometriosis

explanation: Pain that worsens progressively and resists standard NSAID therapy points toward secondary dysmenorrhea, with endometriosis being a primary differential. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h4)

question: What is considered the gold standard diagnostic procedure for confirming a definitive diagnosis of endometriosis?

options.A: Hysterosalpingography using radiopaque contrast
options.B: Serum CA-125 tumor marker blood level assay
options.C: Diagnostic laparoscopy with histological tissue biopsy
options.D: Routine transabdominal pelvic ultrasound scanning

explanation: Direct visualization via laparoscopy combined with microscopic confirmation of endometrial glands and stroma remains the definitive diagnostic standard. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h5)

question: Why might a patient with severe pelvic pain have completely normal results on a standard transvaginal ultrasound?

options.A: Endometriosis tissue dissolves instantly when exposed to high-frequency sound waves
options.B: Ultrasound waves cannot penetrate the pelvic cavity during menstruation
options.C: Imaging only detects lesions that have metastasized to the lungs or liver
options.D: Superficial peritoneal implants are typically too small to visualize on imaging

explanation: Standard imaging modalities easily spot large cysts or deep nodules, but flat, superficial peritoneal lesions generally evade visualization. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h5)

question: What is the primary pharmacological objective of using GnRH agonists in the treatment of endometriosis?

options.A: To completely eliminate systemic progesterone resistance in the uterus
options.B: To permanently stimulate bilateral ovarian follicular development
options.C: To induce temporary medical menopause and suppress estrogen production
options.D: To dissolve pelvic scar tissue through direct enzymatic action

explanation: GnRH agonists downregulate the pituitary-ovarian axis, dropping estrogen levels to starve and shrink estrogen-dependent endometrial implants. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h6)

question: When is a definitive surgical approach involving a hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy typically considered?

options.A: Whenever a patient experiences mild dysmenorrhea during her initial menstrual cycles
options.B: As the mandatory first-line therapy for all adolescent girls newly diagnosed with the condition
options.C: For patients with severe disease who have completed childbearing and failed conservative treatments
options.D: Exclusively to treat asymptomatic superficial peritoneal lesions discovered incidentally

explanation: Definitive surgery is reserved for severe, refractory cases where future fertility is no longer desired, as it removes the hormonal source driving the disease. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h6)

question: Which nursing intervention is most appropriate for a patient experiencing chronic pelvic pain from endometriosis?

options.A: Encouraging complete bed rest to prevent any movement of pelvic organs
options.B: Assessing pain regularly using a validated scale and evaluating treatment effectiveness
options.C: Telling the client that menstrual pain is a standard experience requiring no analgesia
options.D: Advising the patient to discontinue hormonal therapy immediately if mild spotting occurs

explanation: Systematic pain assessment ensures that interventions are working and allows nurses to advocate for timely therapy adjustments. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h7)

question: Why is psychological support a critical component of holistic nursing care for clients with endometriosis?

options.A: Psychological interventions completely replace the need for any hormonal or surgical therapy
options.B: Emotional counseling can physically dissolve deep infiltrating endometriotic nodules
options.C: Mental health distress is the sole physiological trigger for retrograde menstruation
options.D: Chronic pain and fertility concerns frequently contribute to anxiety and depression

explanation: The chronic, unpredictable nature of pain combined with reproductive challenges places a heavy psychological burden on patients, requiring targeted emotional support. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h7)

question: How do ovarian endometriomas typically threaten a patient's fertility?

options.A: By directly converting all normal estrogen into excessive amounts of testosterone
options.B: By increasing the basal metabolic rate and preventing embryo implantation
options.C: By blocking the transmission of nerve impulses through the spinal cord
options.D: By destroying surrounding ovarian cortex tissue and reducing ovarian reserve

explanation: Endometriomas occupy space and create local inflammatory pressure that diminishes the pool of healthy follicles within the ovary. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h8)

question: A patient with Stage IV endometriosis asks why she is experiencing difficulty conceiving even though her uterus is healthy. What is the best nursing explanation?

options.A: Endometrial cells inside the uterus prevent sperm from entering the cervical canal
options.B: Pelvic adhesions and anatomical distortion can block the fallopian tubes and impair egg transport
options.C: Implanted lesions release hormones that instantly destroy all male sperm cells
options.D: The condition causes complete cessation of ovulation in every natural cycle

explanation: Scar tissue and structural distortion physically interfere with the normal pickup and passage of eggs through the reproductive tract. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h8)

question: What is the primary cellular origin of uterine fibroids?

options.A: Smooth muscle cells of the myometrium
options.B: Glandular cells of the endometrium
options.C: Squamous cells of the cervix
options.D: Endothelial cells of uterine blood vessels

explanation: Leiomyomas originate specifically from the myometrium, which is the muscular middle layer of the uterine wall. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h1)

question: Why do uterine fibroids typically shrink following menopause?

options.A: Uterine ligament calcification blocking growth
options.B: Decline in circulating ovarian estrogen and progesterone
options.C: Complete atrophy of the endometrial cavity
options.D: Surgical cessation of local pelvic blood flow

explanation: Because myomas are hormone-dependent tumors, the drastic drop in reproductive hormones post-menopause removes the stimulus for cellular proliferation. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h1)

question: Which classification describes a fibroid that develops directly beneath the inner mucosal lining of the uterus?

options.A: Submucosal
options.B: Subserosal
options.C: Pedunculated
options.D: Intramural

explanation: Submucosal fibroids sit right under the endometrium and project into the uterine cavity, frequently causing heavy menstrual bleeding. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h2)

question: A patient presents with a fibroid located completely within the muscular wall without distorting the outer or inner contours. What type is this?

options.A: Broad ligament
options.B: Cervical
options.C: Subserosal
options.D: Intramural

explanation: Intramural fibroids grow strictly within the myometrium itself, staying contained inside the muscular walls of the uterine body. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h2)

question: Which demographic group experiences the highest incidence and earlier onset of uterine fibroids?

options.A: Post-menopausal Caucasian women
options.B: Nulliparous adolescent females
options.C: Asian women over sixty years old
options.D: Women of African descent

explanation: Epidemiological data consistently shows that black women develop fibroids earlier and suffer a greater burden of disease. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h3)

question: Which factor is most directly associated with an increased risk of developing myomas?

options.A: High dietary intake of complex carbohydrates
options.B: Prolonged lifetime exposure to estrogen and progesterone
options.C: Chronic bacterial infections of the lower urinary tract
options.D: Frequent participation in high-impact aerobic exercise

explanation: Factors that increase cumulative hormonal exposure, such as early menarche and late menopause, elevate the likelihood of fibroid formation. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h3)

question: What is the term for excessively heavy and prolonged menstrual bleeding commonly caused by submucosal fibroids?

options.A: Dysmenorrhea
options.B: Amenorrhea
options.C: Menorrhagia
options.D: Metrorrhagia

explanation: Menorrhagia describes abnormally heavy or prolonged periods, a hallmark symptom frequently linked to submucosal myomas disrupting the endometrium. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h4)

question: Why do patients with large anterior uterine fibroids frequently complain of urinary frequency?

options.A: Associated pelvic inflammatory disease obstructs the ureters
options.B: Hormonal imbalances directly irritate the renal pelvis
options.C: Increased estrogen production causes systemic fluid retention
options.D: The mass effect of the tumor compresses the urinary bladder

explanation: An anatomically enlarged uterus or anterior fibroid physically encroaches on bladder space, reducing storage capacity and triggering frequent urination. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h4)

question: What is the primary imaging modality used to diagnose and map uterine fibroids?

options.A: Computed tomography scan
options.B: Intravenous pyelogram
options.C: Abdominal radiograph
options.D: Pelvic ultrasound

explanation: Pelvic ultrasound is safe, non-invasive, and highly effective at visualizing uterine masses and determining their location. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h5)

question: A patient with multiple large fibroids presents with severe fatigue, pale conjunctiva, and a hemoglobin level of 8 g/dL. What is the immediate nursing priority?

options.A: Encourage high-intensity aerobic exercise to improve cardiovascular tone
options.B: Prepare the patient for immediate total abdominal hysterectomy
options.C: Administer oral contraceptives to immediately stop the menstrual cycle
options.D: Assess for signs of anemia and report findings for medical intervention

explanation: Severe menorrhagia from fibroids often results in critical anemia, making identification and prompt management of low hemoglobin the immediate clinical priority. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h5)

question: Which surgical procedure removes uterine fibroids while preserving the uterus for future childbearing?

options.A: Hysterectomy
options.B: Salpingectomy
options.C: Oophorectomy
options.D: Myomectomy

explanation: A myomectomy is specifically designed to excise the fibroid tumors while leaving the uterine structure intact for potential future pregnancies. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h6)

question: What is the primary clinical purpose of administering a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist prior to fibroid surgery?

options.A: To eliminate the need for general anesthesia during the procedure
options.B: To permanently prevent future recurrence of benign myomas
options.C: To induce temporary hypoestrogenism and reduce tumor volume
options.D: To stimulate rapid endometrial shedding and prevent heavy bleeding

explanation: GnRH agonists suppress ovarian hormone production, creating a low-estrogen environment that temporarily shrinks the fibroids to ease surgical resection. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h6)

question: Which type of fibroid is most directly associated with implantation failure and infertility?

options.A: Pedunculated serosal
options.B: Submucosal
options.C: Subserosal
options.D: Broad ligament

explanation: Submucosal fibroids directly distort the uterine cavity lining, creating an unfavorable environment for embryo implantation. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h7)

question: What pathological process explains the sudden onset of severe localized pain in a growing fibroid during pregnancy?

options.A: Acute bacterial infection tracking from the cervix
options.B: Red degeneration due to cellular ischemia and necrosis
options.C: Malicious malignant transformation into a leiomyosarcoma
options.D: Spontaneous rupture of the outer peritoneal capsule

explanation: When a fibroid outgrows its blood supply, it undergoes ischemic infarction, commonly referred to as red or carneous degeneration, causing acute pain. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h7)

question: What is the most common histological type of uterine cancer?

options.A: Uterine sarcoma
options.B: Leiomyosarcoma
options.C: Squamous cell carcinoma
options.D: Endometrial carcinoma

explanation: Endometrial carcinoma originates in the inner lining of the uterus and makes up the vast majority of all uterine cancer cases. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h1)

question: Why does uterine cancer often have a favorable early-stage prognosis?

options.A: Symptoms like abnormal bleeding appear early, prompting timely investigation
options.B: Malignant cells in the endometrium are inherently slow-growing
options.C: The muscular wall prevents any metastasis until very late stages
options.D: Routine screening blood tests detect cellular changes before tumors form

explanation: Because the inner lining sheds or bleeds when disrupted by a tumor, women notice abnormal bleeding early and seek care before widespread spread occurs. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h1)

question: Which classification of endometrial cancer is typically estrogen-dependent and low-grade?

options.A: Type IV
options.B: Type II
options.C: Type I
options.D: Type III

explanation: Type I endometrial cancers are common, estrogen-driven, and tend to have a less aggressive clinical course than Type II tumors. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h2)

question: What distinguishes uterine sarcomas from endometrial adenocarcinomas?

options.A: Sarcomas are strictly benign tumors that only rarely undergo malignant transformation
options.B: Sarcomas respond completely to oral hormonal replacement therapy
options.C: Sarcomas arise from the muscular wall or connective tissue rather than the glandular lining
options.D: Sarcomas are exclusively diagnosed in patients under the age of thirty

explanation: While adenocarcinomas originate in the epithelial lining of the uterus, sarcomas develop from the myometrium or stromal connective tissues. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h2)

question: The primary hormonal imbalance that increases endometrial cancer risk is prolonged exposure to unopposed:

options.A: Estrogen
options.B: Prolactin
options.C: Testosterone
options.D: Progesterone

explanation: Unopposed estrogen stimulates uninterrupted endometrial cell division, which is a primary driver for malignant transformation. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h3)

question: A 60-year-old female presents with obesity, nulliparity, and type 2 diabetes. Which condition is she at highest risk of developing?

options.A: Endometrial carcinoma
options.B: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma
options.C: Vaginal clear cell adenocarcinoma
options.D: Ovarian germ cell tumor

explanation: Obesity, nulliparity, and advancing age are classic risk factors specifically associated with endometrial cancer. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h3)

question: What is the most common presenting symptom of uterine cancer?

options.A: Foul-smelling vaginal discharge
options.B: Abnormal vaginal bleeding
options.C: Inability to achieve pregnancy
options.D: Severe lower abdominal cramping

explanation: Unexplained vaginal bleeding or spotting, particularly after menopause, is the primary clinical warning sign of endometrial malignancy. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h4)

question: Why is any vaginal bleeding in a postmenopausal woman treated with high clinical suspicion?

options.A: Postmenopausal women cannot absorb iron adequately if bleeding occurs
options.B: Hormone replacement therapy guarantees total cessation of all mucosal shedding
options.C: Malignant cells completely destroy the vaginal walls within days
options.D: The endometrium should be atrophic after menopause, making bleeding abnormal

explanation: After menopause, estrogen levels drop and the uterine lining becomes thin and inactive, meaning any bleeding indicates pathological disruption. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h4)

question: Which diagnostic procedure provides definitive histological confirmation of uterine cancer?

options.A: Serum CA-125 blood assay
options.B: Endometrial biopsy
options.C: Transvaginal ultrasound
options.D: Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging

explanation: A tissue sample obtained via biopsy or curettage is required to examine cellular architecture and confirm the diagnosis of cancer. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing a transvaginal ultrasound in a patient presenting with postmenopausal bleeding?

options.A: To evaluate liver function and rule out distant metastatic lesions
options.B: To measure endometrial thickness and determine the need for tissue biopsy
options.C: To remove small malignant polyps without invasive surgical procedures
options.D: To visualize cancer cells circulating within the pelvic lymphatics

explanation: Transvaginal ultrasound acts as a non-invasive screening tool; a thin endometrium rules out most cancers, while a thick stripe prompts a biopsy. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h5)

question: What is the standard surgical treatment for early-stage uterine cancer?

options.A: Partial resection of the uterine fundus preserving the ovaries
options.B: Endometrial ablation and hormonal suppression therapy
options.C: Radical vulvectomy with superficial inguinal node dissection
options.D: Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy

explanation: Removal of the entire uterus along with the fallopian tubes and ovaries is the standard surgical management to eliminate the primary tumor and at-risk adnexa. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h6)

question: When is adjuvant radiation or chemotherapy typically recommended following surgery?

options.A: When the tumor is classified as a low-grade, early-stage Type I lesion
options.B: When pathology reveals high-risk features, deep myometrial invasion, or lymph node involvement
options.C: When the patient refuses surgical intervention due to personal preferences
options.D: When the patient desires future fertility preservation despite a malignant diagnosis

explanation: Adjuvant therapies are reserved for cases where pathological indicators suggest a higher likelihood of tumor recurrence or local spread. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h6)

question: What is a key postoperative priority following a total abdominal hysterectomy?

options.A: Encouraging heavy lifting to strengthen abdominal wall muscles
options.B: Restricting oral fluid intake for the first seventy-two hours
options.C: Applying continuous hot packs directly over the lower incision
options.D: Monitoring for hemorrhage and promoting early ambulation

explanation: Close observation for bleeding and early mobilization to prevent venous thromboembolism are critical components of immediate postoperative nursing care. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h7)

question: What information should be included when counseling a patient who has undergone a bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy?

options.A: Guidance on maintaining normal menstrual cycles using oral contraceptives
options.B: Instructions on how to perform daily self-catheterization for bladder spasms
options.C: Precautions regarding dietary restrictions to prevent permanent weight loss
options.D: Discussion regarding the onset of surgical menopause and symptom management

explanation: Removing the ovaries triggers abrupt estrogen withdrawal, leading to menopausal symptoms that patients must be prepared to manage. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h7)

question: What is the single most important prognostic factor in uterine cancer?

options.A: Body mass index prior to surgical intervention
options.B: Stage of the disease at the time of diagnosis
options.C: Presence of a family history of colon cancer
options.D: Patient age at initial symptom presentation

explanation: The extent of disease spread (staging) is the most critical determinant of overall survival and prognosis in uterine malignancies. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h8)

question: Which complication is commonly associated with pelvic lymph node dissection during uterine cancer surgery?

options.A: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
options.B: Spontaneous pathological bone fractures
options.C: Permanent bilateral vocal cord paralysis
options.D: Lower extremity lymphedema

explanation: Disruption or removal of pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes impairs lymphatic drainage, frequently resulting in swelling of the legs. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h8)

question: What is the medical term for inflammation of the fallopian tubes?

options.A: Endometritis
options.B: Oophoritis
options.C: Salpingitis
options.D: Cervicitis

explanation: Salpingitis specifically designates inflammation localized to the fallopian tubes, usually resulting from an ascending bacterial infection. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h1)

question: Why is fallopian tube inflammation rarely viewed as a totally isolated pathology?

options.A: It exclusively develops during the third trimester of pregnancy
options.B: It always spreads rapidly to involve the urinary bladder
options.C: It primarily originates from systemic blood-borne fungal spores
options.D: It usually forms part of a broader pelvic inflammatory disease process

explanation: Infections ascending the reproductive tract typically involve multiple pelvic structures simultaneously, making salpingitis a core component of pelvic inflammatory disease. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h1)

question: Which two sexually transmitted pathogens are most commonly responsible for acute salpingitis?

options.A: Treponema pallidum and Trichomonas vaginalis
options.B: Human Papillomavirus and Herpes Simplex Virus
options.C: Candida albicans and Gardnerella vaginalis
options.D: Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis

explanation: Gonorrhea and chlamydia are the leading bacterial agents responsible for initiating upper female reproductive tract infections. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h2)

question: A patient asks why having multiple sexual partners increases her risk of developing fallopian tube infections. What is the best nursing explanation?

options.A: It raises the statistical exposure to sexually transmitted bacteria that can ascend into the tubes
options.B: It permanently alters the pH balance of the external genitalia
options.C: It accelerates the natural shedding of the uterine lining each month
options.D: It causes hormonal imbalances that weaken the muscular walls of the uterus

explanation: Exposure to multiple partners increases the probability of contracting pathogens like chlamydia and gonorrhea, which subsequently ascend past the cervix. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h2)

question: What term describes a fallopian tube that has become blocked and distended with pus due to severe infection?

options.A: Pyosalpinx
options.B: Hydrosalpinx
options.C: Hematosalpinx
options.D: Salpingolysis

explanation: Pyosalpinx refers to the accumulation of purulent material within an obstructed fallopian tube during advanced inflammation. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h3)

question: How does chronic or recurrent salpingitis ultimately impair normal tubal transport of an ovum?

options.A: By destroying the ciliated epithelium and causing fibrous scar tissue obstruction
options.B: By increasing the production of clear lubricating follicular fluid
options.C: By preventing ovulation from occurring in the adjacent ovary
options.D: By enlarging the overall diameter of the myometrium

explanation: Inflammation destroys the microscopic cilia responsible for sweeping the egg toward the uterus, while scar tissue creates physical roadblocks. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h3)

question: Which physical examination finding is classic for acute pelvic inflammatory conditions like salpingitis?

options.A: Right upper quadrant rigidity
options.B: Positive Murphy's sign
options.C: Cervical motion tenderness
options.D: Hypoactive bowel sounds

explanation: Moving the cervix during a bimanual pelvic exam stretches inflamed pelvic tissues, eliciting sharp pain characteristic of upper tract infection. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h4)

question: A patient presents with bilateral lower abdominal pain, purulent cervical discharge, and fever. Which symptom is she most likely to report regarding her menstrual cycle?

options.A: Intermenstrual spotting or heavier periods
options.B: Regular cycles with decreased flow duration
options.C: Delayed menarche for her age group
options.D: Complete permanent cessation of menses

explanation: Infection and inflammation of the reproductive tract frequently disrupt the normal endometrial lining, leading to irregular bleeding or abnormal spotting. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h4)

question: Which laboratory investigation is commonly ordered to support a clinical suspicion of acute infection and inflammation?

options.A: Fastin blood glucose and HbA1c
options.B: Liver function enzymes and bilirubin
options.C: C-reactive protein and white blood cell count
options.D: Serum electrolyte and creatinine levels

explanation: Elevated inflammatory proteins and white blood cells reflect the body's active immune response to bacterial infection. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) on cervical secretions during a salpingitis workup?

options.A: To evaluate the structural patency of the internal tubal lumen
options.B: To detect specific genetic material of causative organisms like chlamydia or gonorrhea
options.C: To rule out ectopic implantation of a fertilized ovum
options.D: To measure the exact hormonal concentration of circulating progesterone

explanation: NAAT provides high sensitivity and specificity in identifying the exact microbial pathogens responsible for the upper tract infection. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h5)

question: What is the primary medical treatment approach for uncomplicated acute salpingitis?

options.A: Broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy
options.B: Immediate surgical removal of both tubes
options.C: High-dose systemic corticosteroid infusion
options.D: Therapeutic uterine curettage

explanation: Antibiotics targeting the likely bacterial pathogens are the primary treatment to eradicate infection and halt tissue destruction. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h6)

question: When would surgical intervention be prioritized over outpatient antibiotic treatment in a patient with tubal inflammation?

options.A: When a ruptured tubo-ovarian abscess causes acute surgical abdomen signs
options.B: When the patient requests permanent sterilization during the visit
options.C: When laboratory tests show a normal baseline white blood cell count
options.D: When mild lower abdominal discomfort persists for more than two days

explanation: Surgical drainage or excision is mandatory in acute surgical emergencies like abscess rupture, where antibiotics alone are insufficient. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h6)

question: Which nursing action is essential when caring for a hospitalized patient receiving treatment for acute salpingitis?

options.A: Administering prescribed antibiotics strictly on schedule to maintain therapeutic blood levels
options.B: Performing daily bimanual pelvic examinations to measure tubal shrinkage
options.C: Restricting fluid intake completely to prevent lower abdominal bloating
options.D: Encouraging strenuous daily physical exercise to speed up pelvic circulation

explanation: Punctual medication administration ensures continuous bactericidal or bacteriostatic action against the infecting organisms. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h7)

question: Why is partner notification and treatment emphasized as a critical component of nursing discharge instructions?

options.A: To determine the primary source of financial payment for medications
options.B: To prevent recurrent infection from untreated sexual contacts
options.C: To confirm the exact date when sexual activity can resume safely
options.D: To satisfy mandatory administrative hospital reporting quotas

explanation: Treating sexual partners breaks the cycle of reinfection with sexually transmitted pathogens like chlamydia and gonorrhea. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h7)

question: What is a major long-term reproductive complication associated with poorly treated salpingitis?

options.A: Hypertrophy of the external genitalia
options.B: Permanent cessation of all ovarian hormones
options.C: Spontaneous elongation of the uterus
options.D: Ectopic pregnancy and infertility

explanation: Tubal scarring and mucosal destruction obstruct normal ovum transport, leading to high rates of infertility and ectopic implantation. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h8)

question: How does structural damage inside the fallopian tube directly cause an ectopic pregnancy?

options.A: By altering ovarian hormone secretion to induce multiple simultaneous ovulations
options.B: By destroying the myometrium and forcing implantation into the abdominal wall
options.C: By trapping the fertilized egg within the scarred lumen before it reaches the uterine cavity
options.D: By accelerating the transit time of the zygote so it implants prematurely

explanation: Fibrotic narrowing and loss of ciliated movement trap the moving embryo inside the tube, resulting in a tubal ectopic pregnancy. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h8)

question: What is the typical length range of a normal adult human fallopian tube?

options.A: 5 to 7 centimeters
options.B: 20 to 25 centimeters
options.C: 10 to 12 centimeters
options.D: 15 to 18 centimeters

explanation: Normal fallopian tubes measure roughly 10 to 12 cm, providing a standard baseline to identify structural elongations. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h1)

question: In which anatomical segment of the fallopian tube does fertilization most commonly take place?

options.A: Ampulla
options.B: Interstitial segment
options.C: Isthmus
options.D: Fimbriae

explanation: The ampulla is the widest and longest section of the tube, offering the anatomical space and environment required for successful fertilization. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h1)

question: Which embryonic structure gives rise to the fallopian tubes?

options.A: Paramesonephric ducts
options.B: Gonadal ridges
options.C: Mesonephric ducts
options.D: Urogenital sinus

explanation: The paramesonephric ducts, also known as Müllerian ducts, develop into the female reproductive tract, including the fallopian tubes. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h2)

question: How do developmental anomalies of the Müllerian ducts typically present in asymptomatic women?

question: What is the primary consequence of excessive tubular length on ovum transport biomechanics?

question: What term describes female subfertility caused by structural or functional abnormalities of the fallopian tubes?

question: What constitutes the standard clinical timeline for investigating potential infertility in a couple under thirty-five years of age?

question: Why is in-vitro fertilization (IVF) often recommended for patients with severe tubal factor infertility caused by structural elongation?

question: What is a common cause of referred shoulder pain experienced by patients following laparoscopic pelvic surgery?

question: What defines an ectopic pregnancy?

options.C: Group B streptococcus
options.D: Bacterial vaginosis

explanation: Infections that cause pelvic inflammatory disease damage tubal cilia and create scar tissue, obstructing normal ovum transport. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T29#GNS216_U5_T29_h3)

question: A patient asks why she developed an ectopic pregnancy despite using an intrauterine contraceptive device. How should this be explained?

options.A: Intrauterine devices increase the total number of eggs released during ovulation every month.
options.B: The plastic material of the device chemically attracts the fertilized egg into the fallopian tube.
options.C: The device prevents uterine implantation effectively, but does not stop fertilization in the tube.
options.D: The hormonal wires of the device paralyze the muscular walls of the uterus entirely.

explanation: An IUD primarily works locally within the uterus, meaning a fertilized egg can still occasionally implant in the tube if conception occurs. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T29#GNS216_U5_T29_h3)

question: What is the classic clinical triad of symptoms associated with an unruptured ectopic pregnancy?

options.A: Severe hypertension, generalized edema, and proteinuria
options.B: Painless bright red bleeding after the twentieth week of gestation
options.C: High fever, foul-smelling vaginal discharge, and uterine tenderness
options.D: Missed menses, unilateral pelvic pain, and abnormal vaginal bleeding

explanation: The combination of a missed period, localized one-sided pelvic pain, and irregular spotting forms the classic presentation before tubal rupture. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T29#GNS216_U5_T29_h4)

question: A patient with suspected ectopic pregnancy complains of sudden onset right shoulder pain. What physiological mechanism explains this symptom?

options.A: Referred visceral pain radiating along the brachial nerve plexus
options.B: Severe systemic hypotension reducing blood flow to upper extremities
options.C: An acute coexisting musculoskeletal strain from coughing or lifting
options.D: Intra-abdominal blood irritating the undersurface of the diaphragm

explanation: Blood pooling in the peritoneal cavity irritates the phrenic nerve endings on the diaphragm, which refers pain up to the shoulder area. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T29#GNS216_U5_T29_h4)

question: Which diagnostic imaging tool is primarily used to confirm the location of an early ectopic pregnancy?

options.A: Transvaginal ultrasound
options.B: Computed tomography scan
options.C: Magnetic resonance imaging
options.D: Plain abdominal radiograph

explanation: Transvaginal ultrasonography offers high-resolution visualization of the pelvic organs, allowing early identification of extra-uterine gestational sacs. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T29#GNS216_U5_T29_h5)

question: What pattern of serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels is most indicative of an abnormal or ectopic pregnancy?

options.A: Steady, high concentrations remaining completely flat for several months
options.B: Rapid exponential increases that exceed normal limits within 24 hours
options.C: Suboptimal doubling or erratic plateauing over 48 to 72 hours
options.D: Immediate disappearance of the hormone within hours of conception

explanation: Normal pregnancies demonstrate consistent doubling of hCG every two to three days, while failing or ectopic pregnancies show sluggish rises or erratic patterns. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T29#GNS216_U5_T29_h5)

question: What is the primary pharmacological agent used for medical management of an unruptured ectopic pregnancy?

options.A: Prostaglandin E2
options.B: Methotrexate
options.C: Magnesium sulfate
options.D: Oxytocin

explanation: Methotrexate is a folate antagonist that halts rapid cell division, causing the ectopic mass to slowly resorb without surgery in stable patients. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T29#GNS216_U5_T29_h6)

question: When is a salpingectomy chosen over a salpingostomy for treating a tubal ectopic pregnancy?

options.A: When the patient desires future unassisted pregnancies and the tube is completely intact
options.B: When the fallopian tube is severely damaged, bleeding uncontrollably, or rupture has occurred
options.C: When the patient refuses all forms of general and regional surgical anesthesia
options.D: When serum hCG levels are extremely low and declining spontaneously without intervention

explanation: Total removal of the tube (salpingectomy) is necessary when tissue integrity is destroyed or hemorrhage cannot be stopped conservatively. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T29#GNS216_U5_T29_h6)

question: What dietary supplement must patients avoid while undergoing methotrexate therapy for an ectopic pregnancy?

options.A: Folic acid
options.B: Ascorbic acid
options.C: Ferrous sulfate
options.D: Calcium carbonate

explanation: Methotrexate works by blocking folic acid, so consuming extra folate will counteract the medication and cause treatment failure. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T29#GNS216_U5_T29_h7)

question: Why is it necessary to advise patients treated with methotrexate to avoid sexual intercourse until serial hCG tests are negative?

options.A: To eliminate any risk of immediate secondary conception during monitoring
options.B: To prevent uterine contractions or tubal pressure that could trigger a delayed rupture
options.C: To reduce the psychological stress associated with physical intimacy
options.D: To ensure the patient does not experience pelvic infections caused by the drug

explanation: Until the trophoblastic tissue has fully resorbed and hCG is zero, the weakened fallopian tube remains at risk of rupture from physical strain. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T29#GNS216_U5_T29_h7)

question: What is the primary life-threatening complication associated with a ruptured ectopic pregnancy?

options.A: Symptomatic bradycardia from vagal nerve stimulation
options.B: Disseminated intravascular coagulation from infection
options.C: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
options.D: Hypovolemic shock from internal hemorrhage

explanation: Rupture of the fallopian tube leads to rapid, uncontrolled bleeding into the peritoneal cavity, quickly precipitating hypovolemic shock. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T29#GNS216_U5_T29_h8)

question: Which nursing action is MOST critical when a patient with a suspected ruptured ectopic pregnancy shows signs of hemodynamic instability?

options.A: Administering prescribed oral analgesics to control severe abdominal pain
options.B: Applying warm compresses to the lower abdomen to ease muscle cramping
options.C: Assisting the patient to ambulate to the washroom to collect a urine sample
options.D: Establishing large-bore intravenous lines for immediate fluid resuscitation

explanation: Restoring intravascular volume with fluids and blood products is the absolute priority when managing acute hemorrhage and impending shock. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T29#GNS216_U5_T29_h8)

question: What is the medical definition of salpingitis?

options.A: Inflammation of the fallopian tubes
options.B: Ulceration of the cervical os
options.C: Benign tumor of the ovarian cortex
options.D: Infection of the uterine myometrium

explanation: Salpingitis specifically refers to the inflammatory process affecting the fallopian tubes, typically caused by infectious agents spreading upward from the lower reproductive tract. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T30#GNS216_U5_T30_h1)

question: Why does inflammation of the fallopian tubes frequently lead to infertility?

options.A: Damage to the ciliated epithelial lining impairs ovum transport
options.B: Systemic antibodies destroy all circulating spermatozoa instantly
options.C: The ovaries immediately stop producing estrogen and progesterone
options.D: Uterine contractions become permanently paralyzed by toxins

explanation: The inner lining of the tubes relies on delicate cilia to move the egg toward the uterus, and inflammatory damage disrupts this mechanism. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T30#GNS216_U5_T30_h1)

question: Which two bacterial pathogens are the most common causative agents of acute salpingitis?

options.A: Candida albicans and Herpes simplex virus
options.B: Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis
options.C: Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae
options.D: Treponema pallidum and Trichomonas vaginalis

explanation: Gonorrhea and chlamydia are the leading sexually transmitted organisms responsible for ascending upper genital tract infections. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T30#GNS216_U5_T30_h2)

question: What is a major clinical characteristic of chlamydial salpingitis compared to gonococcal infections?

options.A: It exclusively affects postmenopausal women with low estrogen levels
options.B: It produces immediate necrosis of the entire myometrium
options.C: It resolves entirely without antibiotic intervention within forty-eight hours
options.D: It frequently presents with milder, subclinical symptoms that delay care

explanation: Chlamydial infections often cause silent or minimal symptoms, allowing the infection to smolder and cause structural damage before diagnosis. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T30#GNS216_U5_T30_h2)

question: How do infectious microorganisms typically reach the fallopian tubes from the lower genital tract?

options.A: By traveling exclusively through the bloodstream from the pulmonary system
options.B: By migrating across the abdominal wall following surgical trauma
options.C: By ascending continuously through the endocervix and endometrial cavity
options.D: By direct lymphatic drainage from the perineal skin surface

explanation: Salpingitis is primarily an ascending infection where pathogens move upward from the vagina and cervix into the uterus and tubes. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T30#GNS216_U5_T30_h3)

question: What pathological consequence occurs when purulent exudate escapes from the fimbriated ends of the fallopian tubes?

options.A: Systemic bone demineralization
options.B: Immediate renal failure
options.C: Obstruction of the trachea
options.D: Localized pelvic peritonitis

explanation: Infected fluid spilling out of the tubal openings irritates the adjacent peritoneal lining, causing localized pelvic peritonitis. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T30#GNS216_U5_T30_h3)

question: Which symptom is most characteristic of acute salpingitis?

options.A: Bilateral lower abdominal and pelvic pain
options.B: Severe asymmetrical swelling of the lower extremities
options.C: Painless hematuria during early morning hours
options.D: Generalized pruritus over the upper torso

explanation: Inflammation of the fallopian tubes typically manifests as tender, lower abdominal pain felt on both sides of the pelvis. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T30#GNS216_U5_T30_h4)

question: A patient with acute salpingitis is most likely to report which accompanying complaint?

options.A: Complete loss of visual acuity
options.B: Abnormal vaginal discharge and dyspareunia
options.C: Recurrent nosebleeds during physical exertion
options.D: Involuntary muscle spasms in the hands

explanation: Because the infection originates in the reproductive tract, cervical inflammation and tubal tenderness frequently cause abnormal discharge and painful intercourse. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T30#GNS216_U5_T30_h4)

question: What physical examination finding is strongly suggestive of pelvic inflammatory conditions like salpingitis?

options.A: Absence of the patellar deep tendon reflex
options.B: Hyperactive bowel sounds in all quadrants
options.C: Cervical motion tenderness
options.D: Palpable enlargement of the spleen

explanation: Moving the cervix during a bimanual exam stretches inflamed pelvic structures, eliciting sharp pain indicative of upper tract infection. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T30#GNS216_U5_T30_h5)

question: Why is a pregnancy test routinely ordered during the diagnostic evaluation of suspected acute salpingitis?

options.A: To measure baseline human placental lactogen levels
options.B: To determine if the patient requires immediate obstetric delivery
options.C: To confirm embryonic viability prior to antibiotic administration
options.D: To exclude an ectopic pregnancy which presents with similar lower abdominal pain

explanation: Ectopic pregnancies share overlapping symptoms with salpingitis and must be ruled out immediately to prevent life-threatening hemorrhage. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T30#GNS216_U5_T30_h5)

question: What is the primary objective of early medical management in salpingitis?

options.A: Dissolving existing uterine fibroids
options.B: Inducing surgical menopause to halt hormonal fluctuations
options.C: Eradicating infection and preventing permanent tubal damage
options.D: Permanently dilating the internal cervical os

explanation: Prompt antibiotic administration halts the inflammatory cascade, reducing the risk of chronic scarring and infertility. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T30#GNS216_U5_T30_h6)

question: Why is concurrent treatment of sexual partners essential in the management of sexually transmitted salpingitis?

options.A: To prevent reinfection and break the transmission cycle
options.B: To prevent the development of drug allergies in the household
options.C: To ensure compliance with the patient's dietary restrictions
options.D: To normalize the partner's blood pressure levels

explanation: Treating partners stops the ping-pong transmission of sexually transmitted pathogens back to the index patient. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T30#GNS216_U5_T30_h6)

question: Which nursing intervention is most appropriate when caring for a hospitalized patient with acute salpingitis?

options.A: Restricting all fluid intake for forty-eight hours
options.B: Maintaining the patient in a semi-Fowler's position to encourage pelvic drainage
options.C: Encouraging heavy physical exercise to stimulate circulation
options.D: Applying ice packs directly to the lower abdomen continuously

explanation: Semi-Fowler's position utilizes gravity to pool infected exudate in the lower pelvis, preventing generalized intra-abdominal spread. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T30#GNS216_U5_T30_h7)

question: What critical instruction must a nurse emphasize before discharging a patient treated for bacterial salpingitis?

options.A: Avoid drinking water for two hours after taking oral pills
options.B: Perform daily vaginal douches with antiseptic solutions
options.C: Stop medication immediately once pelvic pain decreases
options.D: Complete the entire prescribed course of antibiotics even if symptoms disappear

explanation: Stopping antibiotics early can lead to treatment failure, recurrent infection, and increased antimicrobial resistance. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T30#GNS216_U5_T30_h7)

question: What is a major long-term reproductive complication associated with recurrent or poorly treated salpingitis?

options.A: Permanent ovarian hyperfunction
options.B: Tubal factor infertility
options.C: Hypertrophy of the endometrium
options.D: Hyperplasia of the cervical glands

explanation: Scarring and obstruction of the fallopian tubes prevent sperm and egg from meeting, leading to tubal factor infertility. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T30#GNS216_U5_T30_h8)

question: Why does prior salpingitis significantly increase a patient's risk for an ectopic pregnancy?

options.A: Sperm motility becomes permanently accelerated by residual toxins
options.B: Ova are released at a much faster rate than normal
options.C: The uterus loses its ability to produce progesterone entirely
options.D: Tubal scarring and damaged cilia obstruct the normal transit of a fertilized ovum

explanation: Narrowed tubes and ruined cilia trap the fertilized egg inside the fallopian tube before it can reach the uterine cavity. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T30#GNS216_U5_T30_h8)

question: What is the medical term for inflammation limited specifically to the ovaries?

options.A: Oophoritis
options.B: Endometritis
options.C: Cervicitis
options.D: Salpingitis

explanation: Oophoritis specifically denotes inflammation of the ovarian tissue, whereas the other terms refer to inflammation of the Fallopian tubes, uterine lining, or cervix. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T31#GNS216_U5_T31_h1)

question: Why does oophoritis rarely occur as an isolated, single-organ condition in female patients?

options.A: The ovaries possess a dense fibrous capsule that completely blocks local pathogens from entering
options.B: Ovarian blood supply is entirely separate from the uterine circulation, preventing microbe spread
options.C: Hormonal fluctuations in the pelvis destroy isolated bacteria before they can reach the ovarian cortex
options.D: Infections typically ascend from the lower reproductive tract and involve adjacent structures like the tubes

explanation: Because pathogens usually travel upward from the vagina and cervix, they typically infect the Fallopian tubes and ovaries simultaneously. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T31#GNS216_U5_T31_h1)

question: Which two sexually transmitted pathogens are most frequently responsible for ascending pelvic infections leading to oophoritis?

options.A: Herpes simplex virus and Human papillomavirus
options.B: Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus
options.C: Candida albicans and Trichomonas vaginalis
options.D: Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis

explanation: Gonorrhea and chlamydia are the leading sexually transmitted organisms responsible for initiating upper reproductive tract infections. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T31#GNS216_U5_T31_h2)

question: A patient asks why having an intrauterine device inserted recently increased her risk for pelvic organ inflammation. What is the best clinical explanation?

options.A: Intrauterine devices permanently alter normal systemic white blood cell production
options.B: The plastic material of the device chemically irritates the surface of the ovaries directly
options.C: The procedure can introduce lower tract bacteria past the cervical barrier into the upper structures
options.D: Continuous local pressure from the device stops all blood flow to the Fallopian tubes

explanation: Instrumentation through the cervix can occasionally carry vaginal flora upward into the sterile environment of the uterus and adnexa. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T31#GNS216_U5_T31_h2)

question: Through which anatomical route do most infectious agents travel to reach the ovaries from the lower genital tract?

options.A: Systemic arterial embolization originating in cardiac heart valves
options.B: Retrograde lymphatic drainage directly from the inguinal lymph nodes
options.C: Direct mucosal ascent through the uterus and Fallopian tubes
options.D: Direct trans-abdominal wall penetration from the umbilicus

explanation: Microbes typically move upward from the vagina, through the cervix and uterus, and out through the Fallopian tubes to reach the ovaries. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T31#GNS216_U5_T31_h3)

question: What pathological change occurs within the ovarian tissue during the acute phase of an infection?

options.A: Complete cessation of local blood flow leading to immediate ischemic necrosis
options.B: Hyperplasia of germ cells causing benign cyst enlargement
options.C: Neutrophil infiltration, tissue edema, and localized micro-abscess formation
options.D: Rapid deposition of dense scar tissue that shrinks the entire ovary

explanation: Acute inflammation brings white blood cells, fluid accumulation, and localized tissue breakdown, which can form small pockets of pus. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T31#GNS216_U5_T31_h3)

question: Which symptom is most characteristic of acute ovarian and pelvic inflammation?

options.A: Generalized painless skin rash
options.B: Lower abdominal and pelvic pain
options.C: Chronic persistent constipation
options.D: Upper right quadrant chest pain

explanation: Lower abdominal and pelvic pain is the hallmark symptom reported by patients experiencing inflammation of the ovaries and surrounding adnexa. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T31#GNS216_U5_T31_h4)

question: A patient presents to the clinic with bilateral lower abdominal pain, fever, and abnormal vaginal discharge following a recent infection. Which physical finding would require immediate medical escalation?

options.A: Mild soft tissue swelling in both ankles
options.B: Rebound tenderness and abdominal guarding
options.C: Clear breath sounds throughout all lung fields
options.D: Normal bowel sounds in all four quadrants

explanation: Rebound tenderness and guarding indicate peritoneal irritation, which suggests the infection may be worsening or forming an abscess. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T31#GNS216_U5_T31_h4)

question: What is the physical exam finding where movement of the cervix elicits sharp pelvic pain called?

options.A: Cervical motion tenderness
options.B: McBurney point tenderness
options.C: Cullen sign of the umbilicus
options.D: Rebound peritoneal stiffness

explanation: Cervical motion tenderness, or excitation, is a classic sign of upper reproductive tract inflammation when the pelvic organs are moved during examination. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T31#GNS216_U5_T31_h5)

question: Why are complete blood counts and inflammatory markers ordered during the evaluation of suspected pelvic infections?

options.A: To measure precise circulating hormone levels and predict ovulation dates
options.B: To confirm the presence of an active systemic inflammatory and infectious response
options.C: To screen the patient for underlying genetic bleeding disorders
options.D: To determine if the patient has developed chronic iron-deficiency anemia

explanation: Elevated white blood cell counts, ESR, and CRP provide objective biological evidence that an infection and inflammatory process are active. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T31#GNS216_U5_T31_h5)

question: What is the primary initial medical treatment for acute bacterial oophoritis?

options.A: Therapeutic radiation of the pelvis
options.B: Immediate total surgical hysterectomy
options.C: Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy
options.D: High-dose systemic oral corticosteroids

explanation: Initial management centers on fighting the bacterial infection using broad-spectrum antibiotics before targeted culture results are finalized. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T31#GNS216_U5_T31_h6)

question: When is surgical drainage or intervention typically considered for a patient being treated for pelvic inflammatory complications?

options.A: When a large tubo-ovarian abscess fails to resolve with antibiotic therapy alone
options.B: To prevent normal physiological ovulation from ever occurring again
options.C: As the mandatory first-line treatment for every single case of mild oophoritis
options.D: Only when the patient wishes to immediately enhance her natural fertility

explanation: Abscesses trapped within pelvic tissues often require surgical drainage if medical management alone cannot clear the walled-off infection. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T31#GNS216_U5_T31_h6)

question: Which long-term complication is commonly associated with untreated or recurrent ovarian and tubal inflammation?

options.A: Infertility and ectopic pregnancy
options.B: Chronic progressive bone demineralization
options.C: Permanent systemic hypertension
options.D: Permanent complete loss of vision

explanation: Pelvic scarring and tubal damage significantly impair normal ovum transport, leading to high rates of infertility and ectopic gestation. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T31#GNS216_U5_T31_h7)

question: How do pelvic adhesions from past infections contribute to ectopic pregnancies?

options.A: Scar tissue chemically attracts sperm directly to the peritoneal wall instead of the egg
options.B: Fibrous bands accelerate ciliary beating, pushing the embryo through the uterus too fast
options.C: Adhesions cause the ovaries to stop releasing eggs completely into the abdominal cavity
options.D: Scar tissue distorts and narrows the Fallopian tubes, trapping the fertilized egg outside the uterus
